entities.name: Assisi Cathedral
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Cathedral of San Rufino in Assisi, Italy, consecrated in 1253 by Pope Innocent IV, is the most historically important Romanesque cathedral of Umbria — not primarily for its architecture (though its 12th-century pink limestone facade is one of Italy's finest Romanesque) but because it is where Francis of Assisi and Clare of Assisi were both baptized, making it the baptismal church of both founders of the Franciscan and Poor Clares orders. The font where both were baptized — still present in the cathedral — is one of the most theologically significant baptismal fonts in Christianity.

Francis of Assisi (c. 1181-1226), baptized at San Rufino in 1182, underwent his conversion experience in Assisi at age 20-25 (c. 1201-1206), renouncing his cloth merchant father's wealth at the bishop's court to live in poverty. Clare of Assisi (1194-1253) was also baptized at San Rufino and followed Francis in 1212 to establish the Poor Ladies (Poor Clares). The Franciscan Order, founded 1209, became the largest mendicant religious order in history — currently 25,000+ friars globally.

Assisi's concentration of Franciscan sacred geography: San Rufino (baptisms), San Damiano (Francis's conversion), Porziuncola chapel (Francis's founding community), and the Basilica of San Francesco (Francis's burial place and greatest Gothic cycle by Cimabue and Giotto) make the town the most theologically dense small city in Catholicism. The baptismal font where both Francis and Clare were baptized is preserved behind the high altar — visited by millions annually as part of the Assisi UNESCO pilgrim route.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Assisi Cathedral — housing the baptismal font where both Francis and Clare of Assisi were baptized — is the single most theologically significant baptismal site in Catholic history: the font that initiated two of Christianity's most beloved saints and the founders of religious orders with 25,000+ friars and 20,000+ sisters globally.
